CHAPTER 2.3 · LEARNING AREA 2 · DECEMBER · JANUARY

Equations and formulas

On the left of the balance there are three boxes and two weights, on the right one box and six weights. It is balanced. How heavy is one box? An equation describes exactly such a balance. You learn to solve equations in your head and with equivalence transformations, to translate word problems into equations and to rearrange formulas.

16 LESSONS4 UNITS3 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • solve simple equations in your head: working backwards, trying, thinking it through
  • solve linear equations with equivalence transformations and check the solution
  • solve equations with brackets and fractions
  • translate word problems into equations
  • rearrange formulas for a required quantity

$-4$

$-6$

Which number belongs in the box: $\square \cdot 4 - 8 = 40$?

Backwards: $40 + 8 = 48$, $48 \div 4 = 12$.

Calculate $2 \cdot (3 + 4)$.

$2 \cdot 7 = 14$

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Solving equations in your head

The puzzle “I think of a number, double it and subtract 4. The result is 8.” is already an equation. If you write the number you are thinking of as $x$, it reads: $2 \cdot x - 4 = 8$.

The letter $x$ is called a variable. It stands for a number that we do not know yet. A number that gives a true statement when substituted is a solution of the equation. All the solutions together form the solution set $L$.

KEY POINT · SOLVING EQUATIONS BY THINKING

Working backwards: Undo the steps of the calculation with the inverse operations, starting from the result.

Trying: Substitute cleverly chosen numbers and close in on the solution.

Thinking it through: A product is zero if and only if a factor is zero. A number cubed is negative if the number is negative.

Check: Substitute the solution into the equation. If the statement is true, the solution is correct.

Multiplication dot: Between a number and a variable you may leave it out: $2 \cdot x = 2x$.

No solution: $x \cdot x = -4$ has no solution, because a square is never negative. Then $L = \{\,\}$.

EXAMPLE 1 · BACKWARDS

Solve $2x - 4 = 8$ in your head.

Before subtracting 4 it was $8 + 4 = 12$, before doubling $12 \div 2 = 6$.

Check: $2 \cdot 6 - 4 = 8$ ✓ $L = \{6\}$

EXAMPLE 2 · THINKING IT THROUGH

Solve $x^3 = -8$ and $(x - 1) \cdot (x + 3) = 0$.

$x^3 = -8$: the number must be negative, and $2^3 = 8$. So $x = -2$, because $(-2)^3 = -8$.

The product is zero if $x - 1 = 0$ or $x + 3 = 0$. $L = \{-3, 1\}$

EXERCISES

a) $x + 7 = 3$   b) $x - 5 = -9$   c) $4x = -20$   d) $x \div 3 = -2$

a) $x = -4$   b) $x = -4$   c) $x = -5$   d) $x = -6$

a) $3x + 5 = 20$   b) $2x - 7 = -1$   c) $-x + 4 = 10$

a) $x = 5$   b) $x = 3$   c) $-x = 6$, so $x = -6$

Try the numbers −2, −1, 0, 1, 2: which ones solve a) $x^2 = 4$   b) $x^2 = x$   c) $x \cdot x = -4$?

a) $L = \{-2, 2\}$   b) $L = \{0, 1\}$   c) $L = \{\,\}$

Solve by thinking it through: a) $(x - 2) \cdot (x + 5) = 0$   b) $x \cdot (x - 4) = 0$   c) $x^3 = -1000$

a) $L = \{-5, 2\}$   b) $L = \{0, 4\}$   c) $L = \{-10\}$

Write as an equation and solve: “Three times a number, reduced by 4, is $-10$.”

$3x - 4 = -10$. Backwards: $-10 + 4 = -6$, $-6 \div 3 = -2$. $L = \{-2\}$

TEST YOURSELF!

$x - 8 = -3$

$x = -3 + 8 = 5$

$5x = -35$

$x = -35 \div 5 = -7$

$x^3 = -27$

$(-3)^3 = -27$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Equivalence transformations

The balance: $3x + 2 = x + 6$. Take one box away from both sides: $2x + 2 = 6$. Take two weights away from both sides: $2x = 4$. Halve both sides: $x = 2$. The balance stays balanced the whole time.

When the numbers get difficult, working backwards alone no longer helps. Then you transform the equation step by step until $x$ is on its own on one side.

KEY POINT · EQUIVALENCE TRANSFORMATIONS

The solution set of an equation does not change if on both sides you

  • add or subtract the same number or the same multiple of $x$,
  • multiply by the same number or divide by the same number, as long as it is not zero.

You write the transformation after a vertical line: $\;3x + 4 = 10 \;\;\big|\; -4$

Plan: first all the $x$ terms on one side, then all the numbers on the other, then divide. Finally the check.

Why not by zero? Otherwise $0 \cdot x = 0$ would give any number, and $0 \cdot 2 = 0 \cdot 3$ would give $2 = 3$.

Dividing by a negative number is allowed: $-4x = 12 \;\big|\; \div(-4)$ gives $x = -3$.

INTERACTIVE · THE EQUATION BALANCE
EXAMPLE 3 · VARIABLE ON BOTH SIDES

Solve $3a + 4 = 2a - 8$.

$3a + 4 = 2a - 8 \;\;\big|\; -2a$  →  $a + 4 = -8 \;\;\big|\; -4$  →  $a = -12$

Check: left $3 \cdot (-12) + 4 = -32$, right $2 \cdot (-12) - 8 = -32$ ✓ $L = \{-12\}$

EXAMPLE 4 · DIVIDING BY A NEGATIVE NUMBER

Solve $-4x + 7 = 19$.

$-4x + 7 = 19 \;\;\big|\; -7$  →  $-4x = 12 \;\;\big|\; \div(-4)$  →  $x = -3$

Check: $-4 \cdot (-3) + 7 = 12 + 7 = 19$ ✓ $L = \{-3\}$

EXERCISES

a) $5x - 3 = 12$   b) $7 + 2x = -5$   c) $-3x = 18$   d) $4x + 9 = 1$

a) $x = 3$   b) $x = -6$   c) $x = -6$   d) $x = -2$

a) $6x - 4 = 2x + 8$   b) $5y + 2 = 3y - 6$   c) $9 - z = 2z + 15$

a) $4x = 12$, $x = 3$   b) $2y = -8$, $y = -4$   c) $-6 = 3z$, $z = -2$

a) $0.5x + 1.5 = 4$   b) $1.2x - 0.4 = 0.8x + 1.2$   c) $\tfrac12 x - 3 = \tfrac14 x$

a) $0.5x = 2.5$, $x = 5$   b) $0.4x = 1.6$, $x = 4$   c) $\tfrac14 x = 3$, $x = 12$

Find the mistake: $2x + 6 = 10 \;\big|\; \div 2$  →  $x + 6 = 5$  →  $x = -1$

When dividing, every term must be divided: $x + 3 = 5$, so $x = 2$. Check: $2 \cdot 2 + 6 = 10$ ✓

Solve and interpret: a) $4x + 3 = 4x - 1$   b) $3x + 6 - x = 2x + 6$

a) $| -4x$ gives $3 = -1$, a false statement: no solution, $L = \{\,\}$.   b) $2x + 6 = 2x + 6$, $| -2x$ gives $6 = 6$: every rational number is a solution, $L = \mathbb{Q}$.

TEST YOURSELF!

$2x + 5 = -7$

$2x = -12$, $x = -6$

$7y - 3 = 4y + 9$

$3y = 12$, $y = 4$

$-2x + 1 = 9$

$-2x = 8$, $x = -4$

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Brackets, fractions, word problems

“I subtract 2 from a number and triple the result. The answer is 18.” Here the equation needs brackets: $3 \cdot (x - 2) = 18$. First you subtract, then you triple.

KEY POINT · BRACKETS, FRACTIONS AND WORD PROBLEMS

Remove brackets first: $3 \cdot (x - 2) = 3x - 6$ (distributive law). Get rid of fractions: multiply both sides by the denominator.

Word problems in five steps:

  1. Decide what $x$ stands for: “Let $x$ be …”
  2. Translate the text into an equation.
  3. Solve the equation.
  4. Check against the text, not just against the equation.
  5. Write an answer sentence.

Translating: “3 more” means $x + 3$, “twice” $2x$, “half” $\tfrac{x}{2}$, “reduced by 5” $x - 5$.

Shortcut: With $3 \cdot (x - 2) = 18$ you can also divide by 3 first: $x - 2 = 6$.

EXAMPLE 5 · BRACKETS AND A FRACTION

Solve $3 \cdot (x - 2) = 18$ and $\tfrac{b}{3} + 4 = 14$.

$3x - 6 = 18 \;\big|\; +6$ → $3x = 24 \;\big|\; \div 3$ → $x = 8$

$\tfrac{b}{3} + 4 = 14 \;\big|\; -4$ → $\tfrac{b}{3} = 10 \;\big|\; \cdot 3$ → $b = 30$

EXAMPLE 6 · A RECTANGLE

A rectangle is 3 cm longer than it is wide. Its perimeter is 26 cm. How long are the sides?

Let $x$ be the width in cm; the length is $x + 3$. $\;2x + 2 \cdot (x + 3) = 26$ → $4x + 6 = 26$ → $x = 5$.

Check against the text: 5 cm and 8 cm, perimeter $10 + 16 = 26$ ✓ The rectangle is 5 cm wide and 8 cm long.

EXERCISES

a) $2 \cdot (x + 4) = 14$   b) $-3 \cdot (x - 1) = 12$   c) $5 \cdot (2 - x) = -10$

a) $x = 3$   b) $x - 1 = -4$, $x = -3$   c) $2 - x = -2$, $x = 4$

a) $\tfrac{x}{4} = -3$   b) $\tfrac{x}{2} + 5 = 1$   c) $\tfrac{x + 1}{3} = 4$

a) $x = -12$   b) $\tfrac{x}{2} = -4$, $x = -8$   c) $x + 1 = 12$, $x = 11$

Solve $4 \cdot (x - 3) = 2 \cdot (x + 5)$ and check.

$4x - 12 = 2x + 10$ → $2x = 22$ → $x = 11$. Check: $4 \cdot 8 = 32$ and $2 \cdot 16 = 32$ ✓

Tom is 3 years older than Lea. Together they are 25 years old. How old are the two of them? Write down all five steps.

Let $x$ be Lea’s age. $x + (x + 3) = 25$ → $2x = 22$ → $x = 11$. Check: 11 and 14 make 25 ✓. Lea is 11, Tom is 14 years old.

For a class trip the coach costs €450 and admission €18 per person. Altogether the trip costs €954. How many people are going?

Let $x$ be the number of people. $450 + 18x = 954$ → $18x = 504$ → $x = 28$. Check: $450 + 504 = 954$ ✓. 28 people are going.

TEST YOURSELF!

$2 \cdot (x - 5) = 6$

$x - 5 = 3$, $x = 8$

$\tfrac{x}{5} - 1 = 3$

$\tfrac{x}{5} = 4$, $x = 20$

A number and twice that number add up to $-12$. What is the number?

$x + 2x = -12$, $3x = -12$, $x = -4$

UNIT 44 LESSONS

4Rearranging formulas

A rectangle has $A = 24$ cm² and $a = 4$ cm. How long is $b$? Instead of thinking it through afresh every time, you rearrange the formula $A = a \cdot b$ for $b$ once: $b = \tfrac{A}{a}$. Then you only have to substitute: $b = \tfrac{24}{4} = 6$ cm.

KEY POINT · REARRANGING FORMULAS

You rearrange a formula like an equation. The required quantity plays the role of $x$. You treat all the other quantities like numbers.

Do the same on both sides until the required quantity is on its own. Check the result with numbers.

Example: $\;v = \dfrac{s}{t} \;\big|\; \cdot t\;$ gives $\;v \cdot t = s$, so $\;s = v \cdot t$.

Think about the units: If you substitute $s$ in km and $v$ in $\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$, you get $t$ in hours.

Physics: You need to rearrange formulas all the time in physics, for example with speed and density.

INTERACTIVE · REARRANGING STEP BY STEP
EXAMPLE 7 · THE PERIMETER

Rearrange $u = 2a + 2b$ for $a$. A rectangle has $u = 30$ cm and $b = 4$ cm. How long is $a$?

$u = 2a + 2b \;\big|\; -2b$ → $u - 2b = 2a \;\big|\; \div 2$ → $a = \dfrac{u - 2b}{2}$

$a = \dfrac{30 - 8}{2} = 11$ cm

EXAMPLE 8 · CYCLING TO SCHOOL

Lina cycles at $15\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$ to her school 6 km away. How long does it take her?

From $v = \tfrac{s}{t}$ you get $t = \tfrac{s}{v} = \tfrac{6}{15}\,\text{h} = 0.4\,\text{h}$.

$0.4 \cdot 60 = 24$ minutes

EXERCISES

Rearrange: a) $u = 4a$ for $a$   b) $A = \tfrac12 \cdot g \cdot h$ for $h$   c) $V = a \cdot b \cdot c$ for $b$

a) $a = \tfrac{u}{4}$   b) $h = \tfrac{2A}{g}$   c) $b = \tfrac{V}{a \cdot c}$

A cuboid has $V = 120$ cm³, $a = 6$ cm and $b = 4$ cm. How high is it?

$c = \tfrac{V}{a \cdot b} = \tfrac{120}{24} = 5$ cm

Density: $\varrho = \tfrac{m}{V}$. a) A stone has a mass of 540 g and a volume of 200 cm³. What is its density? b) What volume does 1 kg of gold have ($\varrho = 19.3\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$)?

a) $\varrho = \tfrac{540}{200} = 2.7\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$   b) $V = \tfrac{m}{\varrho} = \tfrac{1000}{19.3} \approx 51.8$ cm³.

A train covers 300 km in 2.5 hours. What is its average speed? How far does it get at this speed in 40 minutes?

$v = \tfrac{300}{2.5} = 120\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$. 40 minutes are $\tfrac23$ h: $s = 120 \cdot \tfrac23 = 80$ km.

In the USA temperatures are measured in degrees Fahrenheit: $F = 1.8 \cdot C + 32$. Rearrange for $C$. How many degrees Celsius are 77 °F? And −4 °F?

$C = \tfrac{F - 32}{1.8}$. $\;\tfrac{77 - 32}{1.8} = \tfrac{45}{1.8} = 25$ °C. $\;\tfrac{-4 - 32}{1.8} = \tfrac{-36}{1.8} = -20$ °C.

TEST YOURSELF!

A rectangle has $A = 36$ cm² and $a = 9$ cm. How long is $b$?

$b = \tfrac{36}{9} = 4$ cm

A rectangle has $u = 30$ cm and $a = 9$ cm. How long is $b$?

$b = \tfrac{30 - 18}{2} = 6$ cm

How many degrees Celsius are 50 °F?

$\tfrac{50 - 32}{1.8} = 10$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

a) $7x = -42$   b) $3 - x = 10$   c) $2 \cdot (x + 3) = x$

a) $x = -6$   b) $x = -7$   c) $2x + 6 = x$, $x = -6$

If you add 15 to a number and halve the result, you get twice the number. What is the number?

$\tfrac{x + 15}{2} = 2x$ → $x + 15 = 4x$ → $15 = 3x$ → $x = 5$. Check: $\tfrac{20}{2} = 10 = 2 \cdot 5$ ✓

Connecting with chapter 1.1: In a triangle $\beta$ is twice as big as $\alpha$, and $\gamma$ is $20^\circ$ bigger than $\alpha$. Calculate all the angles.

$x + 2x + (x + 20) = 180$ → $4x = 160$ → $x = 40$. $\alpha = 40^\circ$, $\beta = 80^\circ$, $\gamma = 60^\circ$.

The area of a trapezium is $A = \tfrac{a + c}{2} \cdot h$. Rearrange for $c$. A trapezium has $A = 30$ cm², $h = 5$ cm and $a = 8$ cm. How long is $c$?

$A = \tfrac{a + c}{2} \cdot h \;\big|\; \cdot 2 \;\big|\; \div h$ → $\tfrac{2A}{h} = a + c \;\big|\; -a$ → $c = \tfrac{2A}{h} - a = \tfrac{60}{5} - 8 = 4$ cm

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Where algebra got its name

Around the year 820, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote a book in Baghdad on solving equations. Its title contains two words that describe exactly what you do in this chapter.

Al-jabr means “completing” or “restoring”: if something is subtracted on one side, you bring it over to the other side, as with $\big|\; +3$. Al-muqabala means “balancing”: whatever is the same on both sides is taken away, as with $\big|\; -2x$. The word jabara also meant setting broken bones.

In 1145 Robert of Chester translated the book into Latin. Al-jabr became algebra. And from the name al-Khwarizmi, in Latin Algoritmi, came a word that you know from computers: algorithm.

Sources: al-Khwarizmi, al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wa-l-muqabala, Baghdad around 820 to 830. Latin translation: Robert of Chester, Liber algebrae et almucabala, Segovia 1145.
